newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels said advancing on Kisangani city.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels said advancing on Kisangani city.

text.p: Rebels pushed on several fronts on Monday towards Zaire's northeastern city of Kisangani, the base of the government army, a regional military source said.
The central government in Kinshasa dismissed a call by rebel leader Laurent Kabila for direct negotiations with President Mobutu Sese Seko as a condition for a ceasefire.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said the government remained firmly committed to a military campaign to retake territory seized by rebels since war erupted in October.
"The position of the government has not changed. We cannot negotiate while foreign troops are on our soil," spokesman Pascal Dema told Reuters.
Zaire accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of sending troops to help the rebels, a charge all three neighbours deny.
A Defence Ministry official in Kinshasa confirmed that the army was battling rebels around Kalima, 50 km (35 miles) east of Kindu, a strategic town with a major airport.
But he played down any immediate threat to Kisangani, which Kabila has declared the next target for his guerrillas, who now hold a 1,000-km (600-mile) strip of land in eastern Zaire.
"Kabila is trying to create anxiety. He declares that this or that town has fallen, knowing that this is false," said the official who asked not to be named.
He said contrary to Kabila's claims, Kindu was still in the hands of the army.
At the Vatican, Pope John Paul appealed on Monday for an end to fighting in eastern Zaire, saying conditions there were "an insult to human dignity".

"No man of goodwill can ignore the fate of these people who, in the regions touched by violence, live in conditions which are an insult to human dignity and where life is constantly endangered," he said in a speech to Zairean bishops.
Kabila says his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire is aiming at Kisangani, a key port on the Zaire river and Zaire's third largest city.

A regional military source, who has closely monitored the rebellion in the east since it started in October, said: "Our information is they are advancing on several fronts towards Kisangani. It appears to be a show of strength by the rebels."
"It is also a tactic to disorganise the government forces and their allies already panicking in Kisangani," he added.

The rebels said they captured the town of Lubutu, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, on Saturday. A straight road joins the two towns. Rebels said their forces advancing from the east were closer to Kisangani than the fighters who took Lubutu, but they gave no details.
Kabila on Sunday dimmed hopes for a ceasefire in the war by rejecting South African and U.S. pressure to make a deal.
In his clearest public statement about secret talks in South Africa last week, he said he refused to sign an agreement to end the war to topple Mobutu.

Kabila told a news conference in the eastern border city of Goma his forces were making steady progress on the battlefield and had captured Lubutu, seven km (four miles) from Tingi Tingi, the site of the largest refugee camp in Zaire.

He appealed to the United Nations to help 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees who fled Tingi Tingi last week in fear of an imminent rebel attack. But he insisted there could be no truce without direct negotiations between the rebels and Mobutu.

Mobutu who has ruled Zaire for 31 years has been receiving cancer treatment in Europe for most of the time since last August. He sent a trusted envoy for the talks in South Africa but this week delayed a planned return home from France.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said in Geneva on Monday it had lost trace of the 170,000 refugees in the Zaire jnungle.
Spokesman Kris Janowski said the UNHCR was trying to verify unconfirmed reports from an overflight that the refugees had left Tingi Tingi.
